unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Provide post-procedure instructions to patients as directed by the clinician, using written materials and teach-back to confirm understanding.
- Recognize common warning signs of post-procedure complications, including infection, bleeding, allergic reaction, and circulation changes.
- Report patient concerns, symptoms, and possible complications to the clinician or supervisor promptly, accurately, and through the correct channel.
- Stay within scope of practice by escalating questions and concerns to licensed staff rather than diagnosing, treating, or advising beyond instructions.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Aftercare instructions are like the teacher's list of rules before a field trip: they tell you what to do and when to ask for help.

### Question 2

The doctor is like the coach who writes the game plan; the assistant helps make sure the player understands and follows it.

### Question 3

When you do not understand a rule, the safe thing is to read it exactly and ask the person in charge, not make up your own version.

### Question 4

A healing cut is like a small garden: you keep it tidy and not too wet so it can grow back strong.

### Question 5

Some rules are different for every person, so you check the note instead of guessing.

### Question 6

A follow-up is like checking your homework the next day to make sure everything is going well and fix mistakes early.

### Question 7

A fever is like a smoke alarm: when it goes off, you tell an adult right away instead of waiting.

### Question 8

If a cut area gets more red, hot, puffy, or oozy, that is a clue germs may be growing there.

### Question 9

A tiny bruise after a shot is like a little fingerprint from the needle, usually nothing to worry about.

### Question 10

Washing hands is like cleaning the table before cooking: it keeps germs from getting where they do not belong.

### Question 11

If a bandage keeps filling with red blood, you tell the doctor fast, like telling a teacher about a spill that will not stop.

### Question 12

Writing down exactly what someone said is like taking good notes in class so nothing important is forgotten.

### Question 13

A needle poke is like a small emergency: you wash the spot and tell the person in charge right away.

### Question 14

Only the doctor decides what a rash is; the assistant is like the helper who takes the question to the doctor.

### Question 15

A written list is like a cheat sheet you take home so you remember every step.

### Question 16

Teach-back is like asking a friend to repeat the directions so you know they will not get lost.

### Question 17

When you are not sure if something is a big deal, ask the person in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 18

Sharp needles go straight into a hard box, like putting broken glass in a safe bin instead of the regular trash.

### Question 19

If a leak will not stop, you call for help instead of just adding more paper towels.

### Question 20

You do not let a friend leave with wrong directions; you check they know the way first.

### Question 21

We talk about a patient's private business quietly, like keeping a friend's secret.

### Question 22

The assistant helps pass along the doctor's plan but never changes it or makes medical decisions.

### Question 23

Some signs mean call for the emergency team right away, like pulling a fire alarm when you see smoke.

### Question 24

Taking a message is like writing a note for the night manager so nothing important is missed.

### Question 25

The assistant is the lookout who spots the warning flag and runs to tell the captain.

### Question 26

Pass along the message exactly, like a relay runner handing off the baton without dropping it.

### Question 27

To decide if a red spot is trouble, you need to know if it is growing, hot, puffy, or oozing.

### Question 28

If the note says 'call when it is too hot,' and someone asks 'how hot is too hot?', you ask the person who wrote the note.

### Question 29

After certain procedures you need a sober, alert driver; the doctor decides when it is safe, not how the patient feels.

### Question 30

Follow the note for when a bandage can come off, and if the note is not clear, ask the doctor.

### Question 31

If the two sides of a cut start to drift apart like a zipper coming unzipped, tell the doctor.

### Question 32

If a body part goes numb, tingly, pale, and cold, that is a red flag, not a normal change.

### Question 33

If pain keeps getting worse even after following the plan, that is a signal to check with the doctor.

### Question 34

If someone gets hives, a puffy face, or trouble breathing, that is like a loud alarm that needs the doctor fast.

### Question 35

A sore, swollen calf after a leg procedure can be a warning that blood is clumping where it should not.

### Question 36

When the note says 'take it slow,' and someone wants an exact day, the doctor picks the day.

### Question 37

When someone lists several clues, you write them all down neatly and hand the list to the doctor.

### Question 38

Even if someone says 'it is probably fine,' you still tell the adult so they can check.

### Question 39

Objective notes are like a camera: they record what happened, not what you think about it.

### Question 40

A good handoff is like a short, clear note: here is what happened, here is what they said, here is what we need.

### Question 41

The doctor set a daily routine; if the patient wants to skip, the assistant checks with the doctor.

### Question 42

If someone cannot keep water down and keeps throwing up, the doctor needs to know quickly.

### Question 43

Only the doctor explains what is causing a symptom, like only the mechanic says what is wrong with the car.

### Question 44

Medicine choices belong to the doctor; the assistant points the question to the right person.

### Question 45

You do not 'fix' the doctor's recipe; you follow it exactly so nothing goes wrong.

### Question 46

If a bandage gets wet, check the instructions or ask the doctor what to do next.

### Question 47

Trouble breathing is always an emergency, like a fire that needs the alarm pulled now.

### Question 48

An urgent message is like a loud bell; you answer it right away even on a busy day.

### Question 49

Use the doctor's own notes to answer 'is this normal?', not guesses or random websites.

### Question 50

Repeat the warning signs word for word so the patient does not miss any.

### Question 51

Wash hands and use fresh gloves like putting on a clean apron before cooking for someone else.

### Question 52

Only the doctor reads and explains test results, like only the coach reads the scoreboard.

### Question 53

Report problems to the person in charge, like telling the teacher instead of whispering to classmates.

### Question 54

Write down what the patient does remember and add a note that the exact time is not clear.

### Question 55

If blood splashes in your eye, rinse it right away and tell your supervisor fast.

### Question 56

The note says how long to keep it up; if the note does not say, ask the doctor.

### Question 57

Saying 'it is nothing' when it might be serious is like saying the smoke is nothing while the fire grows.

### Question 58

Give the doctor the what, when, and how bad, like a good reporter giving the facts.

### Question 59

Changing a bandage cleanly is like making a sandwich with washed hands and clean plates.

### Question 60

Trouble breathing is a fast-answer problem; you get help right away.

### Question 61

Give the patient the written list too, so they have both the spoken directions and a reminder.

### Question 62

A smelly, oozing wound is a warning sign to tell the doctor about, even without a fever.

### Question 63

Write it down right away in the right place, like logging an important event as soon as it happens.

### Question 64

When you are not sure, tell the person in charge right away instead of waiting.

### Question 65

The assistant does not decide 'emergency or not'; they get the doctor or follow the emergency plan.

### Question 66

Feeling dizzy when standing is worth telling the doctor, who will say what to do.

### Question 67

Spot it, write it down, and tell the doctor, like a lookout who reports what they see.

### Question 68

Three small clues together can point to one big problem, like three puzzle pieces that fit together.

### Question 69

In an emergency room of phone calls, trouble breathing always jumps to the front of the line.

### Question 70

If the list says 'call for any of these,' even a small one counts, so you make the call.

### Question 71

Stay on the script and hand anything new to the doctor, like a substitute teacher following the lesson plan.

### Question 72

Chest pain plus trouble breathing after a leg procedure is like a fire alarm; call for help now.

### Question 73

When someone speaks another language, bring in a translator so the message gets across clearly.

### Question 74

A useful report is written down right away in the right place, not passed as gossip.

### Question 75

Pain that gets worse even after following the rules is a sign to check with the doctor soon.

### Question 76

Writing the patient's own words is like quoting them exactly so the doctor gets the real story.

### Question 77

Healing cuts usually need to stay out of pools and lakes until the doctor says it is okay.

### Question 78

If a body part will not move or feels numb, that is a big red flag to report right now.

### Question 79

When you are not sure how fast something needs attention, ask the doctor or follow the office rulebook.

### Question 80

Repeat the rule and, if they need more detail, check with the doctor instead of guessing.

### Question 81

A rash after a new medicine is a clue to tell the doctor, who decides what to do about the medicine.

### Question 82

When a symptom could be big or small, pass it to the doctor and let them decide.

### Question 83

Fingers that look pale and feel cold are a warning sign, like a room getting cold because the heater is off.

### Question 84

The doctor's notes are the trustworthy answer key, not memories or random websites.

### Question 85

A sudden very bad headache after a spine or head procedure is a call-for-help situation.
